# Refrigeration and ice making (`refrigeration`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: helped by piston_pump, air_pump_vacuum, heat_energy_conservation, gas_laws, lathe_screw_cutting
- Core idea: A liquid takes up a great deal of heat when it evaporates; that is why sweat and a wet porous jar cool. A refrigerating machine makes a volatile liquid (ether, ammonia) evaporate at low pressure in a coil inside the cold box, where it draws heat from the contents. A pump sucks the vapour away, compresses it so that it becomes hot, and pushes it through a second coil outside, where it gives its heat to air or water and turns liquid again; it then returns to the cold coil through a narrow valve. Heat is thus pumped from inside to outside at the cost of work on the pump. Without a machine: store winter ice under thick straw or sawdust in a drained pit, cool drinks by dissolving saltpetre in water, or freeze them in a mixture of crushed ice and salt (down to about minus 20 °C).
- Pitfalls:
  - Treating cold as a substance to be added; cooling always means carrying heat away somewhere else
  - Thinking an open refrigerator cools the room; it warms it
  - Leaks: ether vapour explodes, ammonia and sulphur dioxide are poisonous
  - An ice house without drainage; standing meltwater melts the ice quickly
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1780 BC – ice house built for Zimri-Lim of Mari at Terqa; china: c. 1st millennium BC – winter ice harvested and stored (Shijing); iced drinks at court; islamic: domed Persian ice houses (yakhchal) and shallow ponds freezing by night radiation, well attested from the medieval period and probably much older; india: 16th c. – saltpetre dissolved in water to cool drinks at the Mughal court (Ain-i-Akbari); 18th c. ice made in shallow pans near Allahabad and Calcutta; europe: 1550 – Blas Villafranca in Rome publishes cooling with saltpetre; 1589 della Porta freezes with ice and salt; 1756 William Cullen makes ice by evaporating ether under a vacuum pump; 1834 Jacob Perkins's vapour-compression patent (London); 1859 Carré's ammonia absorption machine; 1870s Linde's ammonia compressors; americas: 1806 – Frederic Tudor starts the natural ice trade from Boston; 1851 John Gorrie's air-cycle ice machine patent; 1928–1930 Freon refrigerants (Midgley)
- Read:
  - Oscar Edward Anderson Jr., Refrigeration in America: A History of a New Technology and Its Impact (1953)
  - Tom Shachtman, Absolute Zero and the Conquest of Cold (1999)
